headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage via shared MCP/API workflows; content-writing agent can also create cascading errors from MemMachine outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: MemMachine exposes an MCP Server and REST/Python interfaces, while the content-writing agent can ingest files/stdin and operate in a local development environment. That creates a plausible bridge for attacker-controlled content to be treated as instructions, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF MemMachine output is copied into the content-writing agent's stdin or files, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared MCP or filesystem bridge is introduced, attacker-controlled content can cross agents.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of MemMachine outputs into prompts.
Require manual review before passing any retrieved text to the writing agent.
Restrict the writing agent to a read-only prompt template for external content.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all cross-agent content.
requires-engineering: isolate the agents into separate workspaces.

B_data_leakage.rationale: MemMachine touches long-term user facts and conversational context and has network egress plus MCP/API surfaces. The writing agent handles configuration secrets and can read/write the filesystem. If they share a workspace or the writing agent forwards context to external services, sensitive material can leak; the exact bridge is undocumented, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents share a filesystem or notebook workspace, files containing user facts or secrets can be exposed across agents.
IF the writing agent sends retrieved context to external APIs, secrets in its context window can leave the environment.
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared files before running either agent.
Use separate directories for each agent's working data.
Redact long-term user facts before handing text to the writing agent.
Review outbound API destinations for the writing agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: The writing agent can write the filesystem, execute shell, and spawn subprocesses; MemMachine uses MCP/API access and may also interact with shared local resources through the orchestrator. Even without explicit modify_git_state on either side, overlapping mutable workspace access can still conflict. Because shared-state behavior is not stated, uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory, file overwrites or race conditions can occur.
IF the orchestrator routes both agents to the same mutable resource, one agent can clobber the other's outputs.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same files.
Run one agent at a time for shared artifacts.
Check for lock files before writing.
requires-engineering: add workspace locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: MemMachine can produce retrieved context and conversational outputs, and the writing agent exposes agentic ask/stream endpoints that may consume prior outputs. If the writing agent treats MemMachine text as authoritative, errors can cascade into generated content or actions. No verification step is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF MemMachine output is fed directly into the writing agent's agentic-ask or stream flow, unverified claims can propagate.
IF the writing agent uses retrieved text as source material without citation checks, hallucinations can be amplified.
mitigations: Require source verification before the writing agent acts on MemMachine output.
Insert a human review step for any generated facts.
Limit the writing agent to drafting only, not executing actions.
Log provenance for every cross-agent claim.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates.

E_compliance.rationale: MemMachine is documented as touching long-term user facts and conversational context, while the writing agent handles academic papers, research questions, and configuration secrets. If the pair is used on regulated or residency-sensitive data, retention and disclosure policies may diverge. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated personal data is stored in MemMachine and then copied into the writing agent, retention and disclosure obligations may diverge.
IF the writing agent's logs retain secrets longer than MemMachine's context policy, compliance mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared prompts.
Confirm retention settings for both agents before use.
Delete temporary files after each run.
Keep secrets out of notebooks and transcripts.
requires-engineering: document a joint data-handling policy.
